prompt: Which test tells decorative colour from meaningful colour?

choices.text: Is it one of the brand's colours?
choices.why: Brand colours can be meaningful or decorative.

choices.text: Does it pass a contrast check?
choices.why: A decorative colour can have excellent contrast.

choices.text: Would removing it lose information?
choices.why: Right. If nothing is lost, it is decoration.

choices.text: Is it brighter than the background?
choices.why: Brightness says nothing about meaning.

prompt: Six bars, already named on the axis, each have a different colour. What is the main harm?

choices.text: The chart becomes slower to draw
choices.why: Speed is not the harm.

choices.text: The bars become hard to compare by length
choices.why: Length still works; the colours add noise on top.

choices.text: It breaks the zero baseline
choices.why: Colour does not move the baseline.

choices.text: Readers look for a meaning that is not there
choices.why: Right: groupings, importance, a missing legend.

prompt: Why can only one or two things stand out on a chart?

choices.text: Screens can only show two strong colours
choices.why: Screens show millions of colours.

choices.text: Readers only look at the first two marks
choices.why: They look at everything; they notice first what stands apart.

choices.text: Style guides limit charts to two colours
choices.why: The limit is perception, not a rule book.

choices.text: If everything stands out, nothing does
choices.why: Right. Emphasis is a contrast with what is not emphasised.

prompt: In the highlight technique, what happens to the marks that are not the story?

choices.text: They are removed
choices.why: Without them, North's 60.5% would have nothing to compare with.

choices.text: They get their own bright colours
choices.why: Then nothing stands out.

choices.text: They are drawn smaller
choices.why: Bar size carries the value and must not change.

choices.text: They stay, in grey
choices.why: Right. They are the context that gives the highlight its meaning.

prompt: highlight.py picks the region to colour from the data, as the largest growth. What does that buy?

choices.text: The colour follows the finding when the data changes
choices.why: Right. Next year it points at whichever region grew fastest.

choices.text: It makes the program shorter
choices.why: A name would be shorter; the point is correctness.

choices.text: It works only for the North
choices.why: It works for any region that grows fastest.

choices.text: It sorts the bars
choices.why: Sorting is a separate line.

prompt: A report highlights three of eight bars in three different strong colours. What has happened to the highlight?

choices.text: It is stronger, with three times the emphasis
choices.why: Emphasis divided three ways is weaker, not stronger.

choices.text: It has turned back into a categorical palette
choices.why: Right. One, or at most two, is a highlight.

choices.text: Nothing; any number of highlights works
choices.why: Past two, the eye has no single place to go.

choices.text: The grey bars now stand out instead
choices.why: Grey still recedes; the problem is the three colours competing.

prompt: Between two charts in a report, the Southeast changes from blue to orange. What will readers do?

choices.text: Check the legend again on every chart
choices.why: Once a colour is learnt, readers stop checking.

choices.text: Misread the second chart
choices.why: Right, using the colour they learnt on the first.

choices.text: Ignore the colours
choices.why: Colour is read first; it cannot be ignored.

choices.text: Notice the change at once
choices.why: Nothing on the page warns them.

prompt: Why do colours move between charts when software assigns them?

choices.text: Software picks colours at random each time
choices.why: The assignment is deterministic, by position.

choices.text: The data has changed colour
choices.why: Data has no colour of its own.

choices.text: They follow the order of the series
choices.why: Right. Change the order and the colours change with it.

choices.text: Each chart uses a new palette
choices.why: The palette is the same; the order of use changed.

prompt: How should a program keep each region's colour fixed across charts?

choices.text: Sort the regions alphabetically in every chart
choices.why: That fixes the order only while every region is present.

choices.text: A lookup table keyed by name
choices.why: Right. Names, not positions.

choices.text: Use the library's default colours
choices.why: Defaults are assigned by position.

choices.text: Give every chart a different palette
choices.why: That guarantees the colours move.

prompt: A chart colours the region with the most orders in red. How is it likely to be read?

choices.text: As the best performer
choices.why: Red does not usually read as best.

choices.text: As a neutral highlight
choices.why: Red is rarely neutral in business.

choices.text: As flagging a problem
choices.why: Right. Red reads as bad in most business settings.

choices.text: As the smallest region
choices.why: Colour does not say size here.

prompt: A stock chart shown to an audience in China draws rising prices in green. What might happen?

choices.text: Nothing; green means rising everywhere
choices.why: On many East Asian stock charts, rising is red.

choices.text: The chart becomes impossible to print
choices.why: Printing is not the issue.

choices.text: Readers used to red for rising misread it
choices.why: Right. Colour meanings vary by culture; say them in words.

choices.text: Readers see the prices as stable
choices.why: The issue is reversed meaning, not stability.

prompt: A profit-and-loss chart uses green for profit and red for loss. What change keeps the meaning and works for colour-blind readers?

choices.text: Brighter green and brighter red
choices.why: The pair stays the one most often confused.

choices.text: Blue for profit, red for loss, plus signs
choices.why: Right. Change one hue and add a second cue.

choices.text: Grey for both, with no other change
choices.why: Then nothing tells profit from loss.

choices.text: Green for loss and red for profit
choices.why: That reverses the meaning and keeps the problem.

prompt: Find each part of this highlighted bar chart.

labels.text: the bar the chart is about
where the title states the finding
where the highlighted value is written

hint: The finding goes in words at the top.

prompt: Match each use of colour to whether it is meaningful.

pairs.left: a different colour per named bar
one bar in red among grey ones
five series in five hues on one line chart

prompt: Colour that carries no information, such as a different hue on every named bar, is called ___ colour.
Put the steps of the highlight technique in order.
items: Decide what the chart is about
Colour the one mark that is the story
State the finding in the title

prompt: When is a semantic colour, such as green for vegetables, a good choice?

choices.text: Whenever the brand allows it
choices.why: The brand does not decide what the colour means to readers.

choices.text: When the data matches the meaning
choices.why: Right. The reader decodes it before reading the legend.

choices.text: When there is no legend
choices.why: A legend is still wise if the audience is mixed.

choices.text: When the chart has many categories
choices.why: The number of categories does not decide it.
